21.body: Peak Tracking is tracking the peak central wavelength shift over time (over #sweep). Because of the FSR feature of the resonator, the trace can be out of the sweep range. Usually, the read dataset contains noises or unavailable peaks. The algorithm can: Compute the full-length overall peak shift trace; Or, compute a few trace sections, and decide their relative position later.
21.title: Peak Tracking

22.body: In curve fitting, we already have the 5D vector form of peak representation. This section describes the data structure to store all the peaks in an experiment.
22.breadcrumbs: Peak Tracking » Peak Representation » Peak Representation
22.title: Peak Representation

23.body: The ragged array representation uses two subscripts to locate a peak. peak = ragged_array[sweep_index][peak_index_in_sweep] Notice that some sweeps may have no peaks at all.
23.breadcrumbs: Peak Tracking » Peak Representation » Ragged Array » Ragged Array
23.title: Ragged Array

24.body:
There are actually two parts in the graph representation: A 1D array storing all the peak vectors. A 2D array (adjacency matrix) storing all the peak connections. The graph 1D array uses a single subscript to locate a peak. peak = graph_1d_array[index] The graph 2D adjacency matrix uses two subscripts to describe the connection between two peaks. connection = adjacency_matrix[peak1_index][peak2_index] # the cost from peak1 to peak2
connection = adjacency_matrix[peak2_index][peak1_index] # the cost from peak2 to peak1, if connection is directed
24.breadcrumbs: Peak Tracking » Peak Representation » Graph » Graph
24.title: Graph

25.body: How the adjacency matrix is constructed will directly affect the path finding result.
25.breadcrumbs: Peak Tracking » Construct Adjacency Matrix » Construct Adjacency Matrix
25.title: Construct Adjacency Matrix

26.body:
One simple idea is to only build connections for a pair of peaks between two adjacent sweeps. # demo pseudo-code
from itertools import pairwise, product for sweep1,sweep2 in pairwise(ragged_array): for peak1,peak2 in product(sweep1,sweep2): adjacency_matrix[index_of(peak1)][index_of(peak2)] = cost_function(peak1,peak2) Notice that in the above example, if a sweep has no peak, there will be no connections between the sweep before the no-peak sweep and the sweep after the no-peak sweep.
26.breadcrumbs: Peak Tracking » Construct Adjacency Matrix » A Simple Idea
26.title: A Simple Idea

50.title: @property

51.body: Prerequisite: Interface (OOP) A subclass can implement such interfaces defined in the base class by implementing the abstract methods after inheriting from the base class. The base class can provide a default implementation or not.
51.title: Abstract Base Class (ABC)

52.body: If the base class has no default implementation, the @abstractmethod can enforce the subclass to implement the method.
52.title: @abstractmethod

53.body: @staticmethod works like a namespace. Static methods neither need to know the class nor an instance. It could be used as an alternative way to initialize a dataclass .
53.title: @staticmethod

54.body: Run the code below and figure out why the error occurs. Open it in an IDE and see the linting. from abc import ABCMeta, abstractmethod class Shape(metaclass=ABCMeta): @abstractmethod def print_info(self): ... @property @abstractmethod def area(self) -> float: ... @staticmethod def compare_area(shape1: "Shape", shape2: "Shape"): if shape1.area > shape2.area: print( f"This {shape1.__class__.__name__} is bigger than that {shape2.__class__.__name__}" ) elif shape1.area < shape2.area: print( f"That {shape2.__class__.__name__} is bigger than this {shape1.__class__.__name__}" ) else: print("They are the same size") class UnknownShape(Shape): def __init__(self): self.__area = None def print_info(self): print(f"Unknown Shape with area {self.area}") @property def area(self): return self.__area @area.setter def area(self, area: float): if area < 0: raise ValueError("Area cannot be negative") else: self.__area = area class Rectangle(Shape): def __init__(self, width: float, height: float): self.__width = width self.__height = height def print_info(self): print(f"Rectangle: {self.__width} x {self.__height}") @property def area(self): return self.__width * self.__height class Triangle(Shape): def __init__(self, base: float, height: float): self.__base = base self.__height = height def print_info(self): print(f"Triangle: {self.__base} x {self.__height}") @property def area(self): return self.__base * self.__height / 2 class Circle(Shape): def __init__(self, radius: float): self.__radius = radius def print_info(self): print(f"Circle: {self.__radius}") @property def area(self): return self.__radius * self.__radius * 3.14 if __name__ == "__main__": # inheritance demo shapes: list[Shape] = [ Rectangle(2, 3), Triangle(3, 4), Circle(2), ] for shape in shapes: shape.print_info() print(f"Area: {shape.area}") # shape.area = 0 # Try uncommenting this line # AttributeError: property 'area' of 'Rectangle' object has no setter print("------") print() # static method print("-----static method demo-----") Shape.compare_area(shapes[0], shapes[1]) Shape.compare_area(shapes[1], shapes[2]) print() # property setter demo print("-----property setter demo-----") unknown_shape = UnknownShape() if unknown_shape.area is float: print("This will not be printed because area is None") unknown_shape.print_info() unknown_shape.area = 100 unknown_shape.print_info() # validity check by setter: unknown_shape.area = -100 # ValueError: Area cannot be negative unknown_shape.print_info() # abstract class demo print("-----abstract class demo-----") shape = Shape() # TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class...

55.body: @dataclass Sometimes it is useful to have a data type similar to the Pascal “record” or C “struct”, bundling together a few named data items. Unlike normal class, it's not convenient to define data class properties as private, as the properties are aimed to be exposed to callers. The frozen parameter can set the data class properties to readonly.
